hook.line: In a debate, jumping straight to "no" makes you sound like you did not listen. People who argue well nod first, then push back.
hook.es: Puede que tengas razón, pero yo lo veo distinto.
hook.en: You may be right, but I see it differently.

examples.es: Ya, pero eso cuesta mucha plata.
examples.en: Sure, but that costs a lot of money.

examples.es: De acuerdo, pero hay que pensarlo bien.
examples.en: All right, but we need to think it through.

examples.es: Puede que tengas razón, pero yo lo veo distinto.
examples.en: You may be right (to a friend), but I see it differently.

examples.es: Puede que usted tenga razón, pero el barrio no está de acuerdo.
examples.en: You may be right (formal), but the neighbourhood does not agree.

examples.es: No dudo que la mayoría esté contenta, pero mi experiencia fue otra.
examples.en: I don't doubt that most people are happy, but my experience was different.

examples.es: No dudo que el proyecto sea bueno, pero es muy caro.
examples.en: I don't doubt that the project is good, but it's very expensive.

rule:
Give the other person a point, then say your *pero*. There are three levels.

Casual: *Ya, pero…* or *De acuerdo, pero…*
Neutral: *Puede que tengas razón, pero…*
Formal: *No dudo que…, pero…*

After *puede que* and *no dudo que*, the verb takes its "maybe" form: *tengas*, *tenga*, *esté*, *sea*. You are granting the point, not swearing to it. After *ya* and *de acuerdo* the sentence is ordinary.

English says "but" and gets on with it. Spanish usually pays a small compliment first. Skip it and you sound combative.
smallPrint: Teachers call this a concession: you accept part of the other view before you counter it.

readAndPick.es: Ya, pero eso cuesta mucha plata.
options: Yes, and that costs a lot of money.
No, that costs a lot of money.
Sure, but that costs a lot of money.

readAndPick.es: De acuerdo, pero hay que pensarlo bien.
options: I disagree, and we need to think it through.
All right, but we need to think it through.
All right, so there is no need to think.

readAndPick.es: Puede que tengas razón, pero yo lo veo distinto.
options: You may be right, but I see it differently.
I may be right, but you see it differently.
You are right, and I see it the same way.

readAndPick.es: No dudo que la mayoría esté contenta, pero mi experiencia fue otra.
options: I doubt that most people are happy, but my experience was different.
I don't doubt that most people are happy, and my experience was the same.
I don't doubt that most people are happy, but my experience was different.

readAndPick.es: Puede que usted tenga razón, pero el barrio no está de acuerdo.
options: You may be right (to a friend), but the neighbourhood does not agree.
You may be right (formal), but the neighbourhood does not agree.
The neighbourhood may be right, but you do not agree.

readAndPick.es: No dudo que el proyecto sea bueno, pero es muy caro.
options: I don't doubt that the project is good, but it's very expensive.
I doubt that the project is good, and it's very expensive.
I don't doubt that the project is good, so it's cheap.

readAndPick.es: De acuerdo, pero primero hablemos con Hernando.
options: All right, and I already talked to Hernando.
I disagree, but let's talk to Hernando.
All right, but let's talk to Hernando first.

readAndPick.es: Puede que Vale tenga razón, pero yo no estoy convencido.
options: Vale may be right, and I'm convinced (a man speaking).
Vale may be right, but I'm not convinced (a man speaking).
Vale is right, but I'm not convinced (a man speaking).

yourTurn.prompt: Type the whole sentence, choosing *sea* or *es*: No dudo que el plan ___ bueno, pero es caro.
yourTurn.answer: No dudo que el plan sea bueno, pero es caro.
yourTurn.why: After *no dudo que* the verb takes its "maybe" form: *sea*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type the whole sentence, choosing *tienes* or *tengas*: Puede que ___ razón, pero yo lo veo distinto.
yourTurn.answer: Puede que tengas razón, pero yo lo veo distinto.
yourTurn.why: After *puede que* the verb takes its "maybe" form: *tengas*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say it: "Sure, but that costs a lot of money."
yourTurn.answer: Ya, pero eso cuesta mucha plata.
yourTurn.why: *Ya, pero…* is the casual way to nod first.

yourTurn.prompt: Say it to a friend: "You may be right, but we have no money."
yourTurn.answer: Puede que tengas razón, pero no tenemos plata.
yourTurn.why: *Puede que* plus *tengas* grants the point to a friend.

yourTurn.prompt: Say it: "All right, but first let's talk to Hernando."
yourTurn.answer: De acuerdo, pero primero hablemos con Hernando.
yourTurn.why: *De acuerdo, pero…* grants the point and then adds your condition.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it formal, speaking to one person you address as *usted*: Puede que tengas razón, pero yo lo veo distinto.
yourTurn.answer: Puede que usted tenga razón, pero yo lo veo distinto.
yourTurn.why: With *usted* the verb changes from *tengas* to *tenga*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say it: "I don't doubt that Vale is happy, but my experience was different." (Vale is a woman.)
yourTurn.answer: No dudo que Vale esté contenta, pero mi experiencia fue otra.
yourTurn.why: *No dudo que* is the formal nod, and *esté* is the "maybe" form.

pitfalls.right: Ya, pero eso cuesta mucha plata.
pitfalls.why: Almost. A bare *pero* sounds combative; a small *ya* or *de acuerdo* first makes it a conversation.

pitfalls.wrong: Puede que tienes razón, pero yo lo veo distinto.
pitfalls.right: Puede que tengas razón, pero yo lo veo distinto.
pitfalls.why: Almost. *Puede que* is "maybe", so the verb takes its "maybe" form: *tengas*, not *tienes*.

pitfalls.wrong: No dudo que el proyecto es bueno, pero es muy caro.
pitfalls.right: No dudo que el proyecto sea bueno, pero es muy caro.
pitfalls.why: Almost. You are granting the point, not swearing to it, so after *no dudo que* use *sea*.

personal: Think of something a friend or family member believes that you only half agree with. Say it with *Puede que tengas razón, pero…* and finish the sentence with your own view.
